Goal
* Please clarify when a barista becomes available again after starting a drink. For example, it isn't entirely clear whether a barista who served a drink that started at minute 0 and took 5 minutes becomes free to serve another customer at minute 5 or at minute 6.

Input
* Line 1: Please add "space-separated" after "Two".

* Line 1: Please add the descriptions of [[N]] and [[M]].

* Line 2: Please add "in non-decreasing order".

* Line 3: Please state that [[T]] is measured in minutes.

* Line 3: Please add "The values are listed in the same order as the arrival times on Line 2."

Goal / Input / Constraints / Stub generator
* Please use the same variable names:

  • [[A]] vs [[arrival]]

  • [[T]] vs [[prepTime]]

Output
* Please mention the output is measured in minutes.

Constraints
* Please change 1000 to 10, as [[N]] never exceeds 10 in the cases.

* Please change 10⁶ to 100, as [[A]] never exceeds 100 in the cases.

* Please delete "i" after [[A]] and [[T]] to be consistent with the Input section.

Cases
* Single Barista, Staggered Arrival II (Validator 3): Please sort the order of Line 2.

* Please add a pair of cases where [[N]] = [[M]] = 10, and all [[A]] values are the same but not 0.

* Please add a pair of cases where [[M]] > [[N]] and some baristas are idle and have to wait for customers to arrive.

* Please add a pair of cases that exercise the off-by-one situations mentioned in the Goal section at the beginning of this comment. Within each case, include situations where a customer arrives exactly when a barista becomes available and where a customer arrives one minute before a barista becomes available.

Thanks.

Just a quick heads-up regarding the 2 last tests. it seems the data in these actually contains unexpected line breaks and spans multiple lines. In Py, a standard input().split() fails to read all 'N' integers because it only reads the first line. I had to use sys.stdin.read().split() to bypass the line breaks and pass the tests. ;)

I’m evolving this logic from a 'Clash of Code' snippet into a full puzzle. Could you take a look and let me know if the concept is clear and well structured?

There's an existing scheduling puzzle:
https://www.codingame.com/training/easy/the-helpdesk

At first glance, the clash and the puzzle don't appear to be the same problem. However, since both involve assigning work to multiple workers/counters over time and managing queues, please make sure the puzzle derived from the clash wouldn't end up feeling too similar to the existing puzzle.

The number of possible subsets (for [remaining] in your code) is 2^N. For 15, no problem. For 1,000, your current solver will take a million years :)

If you want to keep this code as is, you’ll need to adjust the constraints (15 max.).
If you want to keep N = 1000 (NP-Hard problem that’s unsolvable without a timeout), you’ll definitely need to change the rules of the game to require some sort of greedy sorting method...

a) Some customers might leave the line when their impatience meter is “full” (medium)
b) Limited equipment: A drink requires several steps (e.g., 1 min. at the grinder, 2 min. at the brew machine, 1 min. at the steam wand...). The shop has limited equipment (e.g., 2 grinders, 1 brew machine) & 1 or X Baristas. (Quite "Hard")
